user_class: Independent sports bettors who use multiple prediction platforms
painful_workflow: To verify that a bet was settled fairly, a user must manually cross-reference a platform's displayed result with an unofficial third-party source, hoping the platform executed the settlement logic correctly as they have no cryptographic proof.
unmet_need: A way to independently and programmatically verify bet settlement by checking the existence of a valid Merkle proof for a specific match outcome, without needing to trust the platform's word.
why_now: TxLINE provides signed and Merkle-ized data on Solana, and the Solana runtime allows for cheap verification, but platforms built for the hackathon may not offer users a way to perform this check themselves, creating a standalone verification need.
unresolved_claims: Whether users actively seek out Merkle proofs to audit their own bets, or if this is a need only for professional auditors.
Whether a standalone verification tool would be a standalone product or just a feature of a larger platform.

user_class: Casual sports fan groups (friends, families, co-workers) in disparate locations
painful_workflow: Current group chat or social bracket platforms are static and disconnected from the live match. Fans manually post reactions, share screenshots of scores, and track friend predictions in spreadsheets, leading to a fragmented experience that dies down between goals.
unmet_need: A shared, persistent space where a group's pre-match predictions are automatically compared against live, cryptographically verified match events, creating a permanent, shared record of 'who called it' that fuels conversation in real-time.
why_now: The World Cup is the ultimate global group-viewing event, yet social platforms lack direct integration with a real-time, server-side authoritative data source like TxLINE, leaving the 'shared predictive moment' unserved.
unresolved_claims: Assumption: causal fans care about the cryptographic verifiability of match events in a social context, not just the speed of the update.
Assumption: the pain point is strong enough for users to adopt a new dedicated platform over their existing general-purpose chat apps.

user_class: Semi-professional sports traders managing custom algorithmic strategies
painful_workflow: To trust a data feed for automated trading, a user must build a redundant ingestion pipeline that polls multiple non-Solana APIs and writes a complex reconciliation script to detect anomalies, before their core strategy logic can even begin to execute.
unmet_need: A recognized standard on Solana for 'feed health', where an agent can programmatically query for gaps, anomalies, or verification failures in a TxLINE data stream without needing to write custom logic to compare it against other sources.
why_now: TxLINE introduces a new, single source of cryptographically-signed data on Solana. The first bots built on it will need a standardized way to trust the feed's operational integrity before they can deploy capital, creating a tooling gap.
unresolved_claims: Assumption: TxLINE's own signing is insufficient and traders need a second-order 'health' analysis on top of it.
Assumption: this tool would be a critical dependency for agents, rather than a simple utility function packaged within the agent itself.

user_class: Developers building prediction markets or automated betting agents (Track 1 & 3 builders)
painful_workflow: To develop and test an application on World Cup data in the weeks before the tournament, a developer must create their own scraper or buy a third-party historical data dump, then write a simulator to replay this data as a live stream—a complex, error-prone prerequisite that delays work on the core product.
unmet_need: An off-the-shelf, TxLINE-compatible developer sandbox that replays archival match data into the exact same Solana-native format and cadence as the live feed, enabling one-line integration and testing of their application's state machine.
why_now: The hackathon is only four weeks long and the World Cup is in the future, yet the primary requirement is a functional build using TxLINE. Builders cannot wait for live matches to start; they need a historical simulator to build and demo a polished, end-to-end product.
unresolved_claims: Assumption: TxLINE itself does not already provide such a historical replay endpoint/simulator for developers.
Assumption: the hackathon judging will reward a tool that enables other builds, even though it is itself a developer tool and not a consumer-facing app.
